correctness.rationale: The signed distance profile on the product is the sum of profiles of the one-coordinate marginals. Its maximum and minimum separately split because all coordinate choices coexist, so half the oscillation adds, with exactly the stated normalization. A zero-sum measure on a factor lifts along its anchored coordinate line and has zero other marginals. This proves surjectivity, identifies the kernel as the preimage of the factor kernels and gives the dimension by rank-nullity. The alternating signed rectangle proves strict degeneracy even when factors have trivial kernels. For an equilateral factor the profile is minus lambda times the signed mass. In the zero-sum hyperplane each ordered difference inequality has a point with only that inequality tight, so all are facets. At a vertex the tight pairs join maxima and minima; an intermediate coordinate would leave a free direction modulo constants. A nontrivial two-level cut is uniquely fixed by its tight equalities and zero sum. The convex hull of the embedded factor balls has exactly their embedded vertices, and its polar is the product of their polars, giving the claimed counts including q_i=2 and s=1. Independent exact check `python /workspace/checks.py 4`: a four-cycle factor (already degenerate) times a weighted equilateral triple has factor ranks 2,2 and rank 4; all 1,320 signed contrasts of type 2e_i-e_j-e_k agree. Exact raw profile-difference inequalities on a weighted 2-by-3 quotient section yield 8 vertices and 12 facets. These are corroborations, not the proof for arbitrary factors.

Neither a rank calculation, a projection in the ordinary transportation-cost norm, nor a one-factor face formula on its own implies that identification.

value.rationale: The natural distance-test norm forgets interactions on product metrics. The precise quotient separates the interactions from factor-level degeneracies and determines all remaining norm geometry, not just a rank or a small example. Hamming products give usable exact facet and vertex counts in that quotient and clarify why ordinary transportation-cost geometry is a different problem.
